big: A fund can return 6% a year while its investors earn far less. The fund did nothing wrong. The money came in late and went out early. That difference is the behaviour gap.

lines: My fund shows a 10-year gain of 78%, but my own statement shows a loss. How can that be?
The fund's return and your return can differ, because your money went in and out at different times. Let me replay your ten years.

alt: Two lines: an investor who held through, and an investor who added after a rally and sold after a fall
caps: Made-up fund: ₹100 grows to ₹178 over ten years, with a fall in the middle. Gain: 78%, about 5.9% a year.
Investor 1 puts in ₹1 lakh and holds. Investor 2 starts the same.
After the rally, in year 3, Investor 2 adds another ₹1 lakh at NAV 146.
After the fall, in year 5, Investor 2 sells at NAV 96 and stays out of the recovery.
Per ₹100 put in: ₹178 for one, ₹81 for the other. Same fund.

alt: Two bars: rupees put in and rupees ended with for an investor who held and one who chased
caps: Same fund, same ten years. The holder put in ₹1 lakh. The other investor put in ₹2 lakh.
The second investor's ₹2 lakh bought units at ₹100 and ₹146, and was sold at ₹96.
He ended with about ₹1.62 lakh. The holder ended with ₹1.78 lakh, from half the money.
The fund earned 78%. His money lost about 19%. Timing, not the fund, made the gap.

title: Closing the gap
stops: A smoother fund gives fewer reasons to panic
A SIP kept through a fall narrows the gap
Waiting for an all-clear before restarting
A fund's return is what every holder earns
alt: A shield with true and false statements about behaviour and fund returns
caps: Volatile funds give more reasons to buy late and sell low, so they widen the gap. Smoother funds narrow it.
A steady SIP through the fall, and an adviser who picks up the phone, close it further.
Picking the perfect day or waiting for an all-clear usually widens it.

intro: One data point the lesson cites, from industry data.
rows: Fall in industry AUM in the month
investors kept investing through the fall
note: One month does not prove a habit has changed, but it points the right way. A client's own steadiness still needs hand-holding.

q: A fund gained 78% over ten years. A client put ₹1 lakh in at the start, added ₹1 lakh after a rally and sold everything after a fall. She ended with less than she put in. What explains it?
opts: The fund itself lost money, so the 78% gain shown on its factsheet must be wrong
Funds always pay lower returns to investors who add money after the first year
More of her money went in at high prices, and all of it was sold at a low
The 78% is a gross figure, and costs cut it below zero for any investor who adds money
why: The fund's own return was positive. It is her timing, not the fund's record, that made the loss.
Funds do not pay different returns to different buyers. They have one NAV, and her entry and exit points differ.
Her second ₹1 lakh bought at the peak and the sale came at the low, so her money lost while the fund gained.
Costs are modest next to a 78% gain. They cannot turn the result into a loss; her timing did.

q: An investor bought 1,000 units at NAV 100 and 684.9 units at NAV 146. She sells all of them at NAV 96. About how much does she receive?
opts: About ₹1.92 lakh, since the 96 NAV is 96% of the ₹2 lakh she put in
About ₹1.62 lakh, since 1,684.9 units are sold at a NAV of 96 each
About ₹2.00 lakh, since what she paid in is what she gets back
About ₹1.35 lakh, since the fall from 146 to 96 costs her a third
why: She bought part at 146, not 100, so the 96 NAV is not 96% of what she paid. Units, not rupees, are sold.
1,000 plus 684.9 is 1,684.9 units. Times ₹96 gives about ₹1,61,750, which is less than the ₹2 lakh she put in.
Selling at 96 returns less than she paid for units at 100 and 146. She gets units times the NAV.
The fall from 146 to 96 is about a third, but only on the second purchase. Her first units cost 100.

q: A client with a multi-asset SIP wants to stop it after the fund falls 12% and restart when things feel safe. What is the adviser's best reply?
opts: Agree, because a restart date can be chosen when the news turns calmer again
Agree, but advise a bigger SIP at restart to make up the lost months
Switch the fund to one with higher volatility, so that the gains come back faster
Show that stopping skips cheap units and restarts come late; keep the SIP
why: Calm news usually arrives after prices have already recovered, so restarts tend to come late.
A bigger SIP later buys at higher prices. It does not recover the cheap units that were skipped.
A more volatile fund gives a client more reasons to panic. It would widen the gap, not close it.
The gap comes from skipped buying and late returns. Keeping the SIP through the fall is the habit that closes it.

q: In March 2026, industry AUM fell about 10% yet equity fund inflows stayed near ₹40,000 crore. What does it suggest?
opts: Investors kept investing through a fall, a good sign, though one month is no proof
It proves no investor sold any units that month and that the behaviour gap is gone
It means the market did not fall, since inflows could not stay high if prices were falling
It means funds that fall get more inflows, so a client should wait for a fall to invest
why: Steady inflows during a 10% AUM fall point to calmer behaviour. One month cannot show a lasting change.
Inflows staying high does not show that nobody sold. Some investors will always redeem in a fall.
The 10% AUM fall shows prices did drop. Inflows stayed because many investors kept going.
One month does not make a rule. Waiting for a fall to invest is timing again, which feeds the gap.

pts: The fund's return and your return can differ. Buying after rallies and selling after falls creates the behaviour gap.
Volatile funds widen the gap; smoother funds narrow it. A SIP kept through falls narrows it further.
In March 2026 inflows held near ₹40,000 crore through a 10% AUM drop. Your hand-holding is what closes the gap.
